# From Row Operations to Inverses

Undoing a row operation leads directly to the idea of an inverse matrix

- [Why square matrices?](#why-square-matrices)
- [Reversible means invertible](#an-inverse-undoes-a-matrix-action)
- [Elimination matrices are invertible](#elimination-matrices-are-invertible)
- [Invertible or singular](#invertible-or-singular)

## Why square matrices?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### [Systems and Matrices]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}): rectangular allowed

$$
\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}
$$

- $m$ equations
- $n$ unknowns
- $m$ and $n$ need not agree
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### [Inverses]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}): square throughout

$$
\mat{A}\in\reals^{n\times n}
$$

- $n$ equations
- $n$ unknowns
- a two-sided inverse may exist
:::
:::

A [two-sided inverse]{.alert} must undo $\mat{A}$ in both orders:

$$
\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{A}=\mat{I}_n,
\qquad
\mat{A}\mat{A}^{-1}=\mat{I}_n
$$

::: {.key-point}
This deck focuses on [square matrices]{.alert}; rectangular matrices remain
important and cannot have a two-sided inverse, but they can have
[pseudoinverses]{.alert} (later)
:::

## Reversible means invertible {#an-inverse-undoes-a-matrix-action data-state="goldborder"}

In [Systems and Matrices]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}), [reversible]{.alert} meant that an operation could be undone

For a square matrix $\mat{A}$, the action $\vct{x}\mapsto\mat{A}\vct{x}$ is reversible exactly when another matrix $\mat{A}^{-1}$ undoes it in both directions:

$$
\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{A}\ }
\mat{A}\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{A}^{-1}\ }
\vct{x},
\qquad
\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{A}^{-1}\ }
\mat{A}^{-1}\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{A}\ }
\vct{x}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{A}=\mat{I},
\qquad
\mat{A}\mat{A}^{-1}=\mat{I}
$$

Then $\mat{A}$ is [invertible]{.alert}, or [nonsingular]{.alert}, and $\mat{A}^{-1}$ is its inverse

::: {.key-point}
Our intuitive idea of a [reversible matrix action]{.alert} means multiplication by an [invertible matrix]{.alert}
:::

## Elimination matrices are invertible

Recall from [Systems and Matrices]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#/undoing-restores-the-original-system): $\mat{M}_1$ zeros the first column below its pivot, while $\mat{N}_1$ reverses that elimination stage:

$$
\mat{M}_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\-3&0&1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{N}_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\2&1&0\\3&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

A direct check gives

$$
\mat{N}_1\mat{M}_1=\mat{I}
=\mat{M}_1\mat{N}_1
$$

Now we can write $\mat{N}_1=\mat{M}_1^{-1}$

::: {.key-point}
Each $\mat{M}_j$ is a product of elementary matrices, so it is invertible; its inverse reverses the whole column-elimination stage
:::

## Invertible or singular

For a square matrix $\mat{A}$:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Invertible = nonsingular

$\mat{A}^{-1}$ exists

- every output $\vct{b}=\mat{A}\vct{x}$ has [exactly one input]{.alert} $\vct{x}$
- distinct inputs produce distinct outputs—no information is lost
- in echelon form, [every row and column has a pivot]{.alert}
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Singular

$\mat{A}^{-1}$ does not exist

- some $\vct{b}$ [cannot be reached]{.alert} as $\mat{A}\vct{x}$
- distinct inputs can produce the same output—information is lost
- in echelon form, [at least one row and one column have no pivot]{.alert}
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Use pivots to test invertibility: row-reduce $\mat{A}$ and inspect its echelon form

Some treatments invoke determinants here; [we will defer them]{.alert}

Elimination reveals the pivots directly

A computed determinant can be unreliable when $\mat{A}$ is nearly singular
:::

# Inverse Algebra

An inverse is unique, and order remains essential

- [Left and right inverses must agree](#the-inverse-is-unique)
- [Undo products in reverse order](#undo-products-in-reverse-order)

## Left and right inverses must agree {#the-inverse-is-unique}

Suppose $\mat{B}$ is a [left inverse]{.alert} and $\mat{C}$ is a [right inverse]{.alert} of $\mat{A}$:

$$
\mat{B}\mat{A}=\mat{I},
\qquad
\mat{A}\mat{C}=\mat{I}
$$

Associativity connects them:

$$
\mat{B}
=\mat{B}\mat{I}
=\mat{B}(\mat{A}\mat{C})
=(\mat{B}\mat{A})\mat{C}
=\mat{I}\mat{C}
=\mat{C}
$$

Thus any left inverse and right inverse of the same matrix must agree

::: {.key-point}
A two-sided inverse is therefore [unique]{.alert}; we denote it $\mat{A}^{-1}$

A matrix commutes with its inverse: $\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{A}=\mat{I}=\mat{A}\mat{A}^{-1}$
:::

## Undo products in reverse order

If $\mat{A}$ and $\mat{B}$ are invertible, then

$$
(\mat{A}\mat{B})^{-1}=\mat{B}^{-1}\mat{A}^{-1}
$$

[Associativity]{.alert} lets us regroup without changing the order:

$$
(\mat{A}\mat{B})(\mat{B}^{-1}\mat{A}^{-1})
=\mat{A}\mat{I}\mat{A}^{-1}=\mat{I}
$$

There is no standard matrix quotient $\mat{B}/\mat{A}$: the products
$\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{B}$ and $\mat{B}\mat{A}^{-1}$ generally differ

::: {.key-point}
The rightmost factor acts first; taking an inverse reverses the order
:::

# Compute an Inverse

Gauss–Jordan reduction records the row operations that turn $\mat{A}$ into $\mat{I}$

- [Reduce beside the identity](#reduce-beside-the-identity)
- [Find an inverse](#find-an-inverse)
- [A missing pivot proves singularity](#a-missing-pivot-proves-singularity)

## Reduce beside the identity

Let $\mat{G}$ denote the product of the elementary matrices used in Gauss–Jordan reduction. Every row operation acts on both blocks, so

$$
\mat{G}[\,\mat{A}\mid\mat{I}\,]
=
[\,\mat{G}\mat{A}\mid\mat{G}\,]
=
[\,\mat{I}\mid\mat{G}\,]
$$

The left block gives $\mat{G}\mat{A}=\mat{I}$. Since $\mat{G}$ is invertible, $\mat{A}=\mat{G}^{-1}$; hence $\mat{G}=\mat{A}^{-1}$.

::: {.key-point}
Gaussian elimination solves systems; Gauss–Jordan reduction is useful here because the inverse itself is the goal
:::

## Find an inverse

For $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$,

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1&1&1&0\\2&3&0&1
\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1&1&1&0\\0&1&-2&1
\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
\xrightarrow{R_1\leftarrow R_1-R_2}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1&0&3&-1\\0&1&-2&1
\end{array}\right]
$$

Thus $\mat{A}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}$

---

### Return to our three-equation matrix

For [our three-equation system]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#/each-equation-is-one-dot-product), apply the same forward-elimination steps to both blocks of $[\,\mat{A}\mid\mat{I}\,]$:

::: {.small}
\begin{align*}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
1&2&-1&1&0&0\\
2&-1&1&0&1&0\\
3&1&2&0&0&1
\end{array}
\right]
&\xrightarrow{\substack{R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1\\R_3\leftarrow R_3-3R_1}}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
1&2&-1&1&0&0\\
0&-5&3&-2&1&0\\
0&-5&5&-3&0&1
\end{array}
\right]
\\[0.8em]
&\xrightarrow{R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_2}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
1&2&-1&1&0&0\\
0&-5&3&-2&1&0\\
0&0&2&-1&-1&1
\end{array}
\right].
\end{align*}
:::

The left block is now in row echelon form

---

### Finish the Gauss–Jordan reduction

Continue upward until the left block becomes $\mat{I}$:

::: {.small}
\begin{align*}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
1&2&-1&1&0&0\\
0&-5&3&-2&1&0\\
0&0&2&-1&-1&1
\end{array}
\right]
&\xrightarrow{\substack{R_3\leftarrow \tfrac12R_3\\R_1\leftarrow R_1+R_3\\R_2\leftarrow R_2-3R_3}}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
1&2&0&\tfrac12&-\tfrac12&\tfrac12\\
0&-5&0&-\tfrac12&\tfrac52&-\tfrac32\\
0&0&1&-\tfrac12&-\tfrac12&\tfrac12
\end{array}
\right]
\\[0.8em]
&\xrightarrow{\substack{R_2\leftarrow -\tfrac15R_2\\R_1\leftarrow R_1-2R_2}}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
1&0&0&\tfrac3{10}&\tfrac12&-\tfrac1{10}\\
0&1&0&\tfrac1{10}&-\tfrac12&\tfrac3{10}\\
0&0&1&-\tfrac12&-\tfrac12&\tfrac12
\end{array}
\right].
\end{align*}
:::

::: {.key-point}
The right block is $\mat{A}^{-1}$; for our original $\vct{b}$, $\mat{A}^{-1}\vct{b}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2&1\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}$ recovers the solution
:::

## A missing pivot proves singularity

For $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$,

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1&2&1&0\\2&4&0&1
\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1&2&1&0\\0&0&-2&1
\end{array}\right]
$$

The left block cannot become $\mat{I}$: its second pivot is missing

::: {.key-point}
Failure is information: the matrix is singular, so no inverse exists
:::

# Invertibility and Linear Systems

One structural property controls every system $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$

- [One theorem, many viewpoints](#one-theorem-many-viewpoints)
- [Reversible versus information-losing](#reversible-versus-information-losing)
- [The right-hand side decides](#the-right-hand-side-decides)
- [Choose the least computation](#choose-the-least-computation)

## One theorem, many viewpoints

For a square $n\times n$ matrix $\mat{A}$, these statements are equivalent:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- $\mat{A}$ is invertible
- $\mat{A}$ row-reduces to $\mat{I}$
- an echelon form of $\mat{A}$ has $n$ pivots
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}$ has only $\vct{x}=\vct{0}$
- $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ has exactly one solution for every $\vct{b}$
- $\mat{A}$ is a product of elementary matrices
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
These are algebraic, computational, and geometric views of [reversibility]{.alert}
:::

## Reversible versus information-losing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### $\mat{A}$ invertible

No pivot is missing, so

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\vct{x}=\vct{0}
$$

For every $\vct{b}$,

$$
\vct{x}=\mat{A}^{-1}\vct{b}
$$

exists and is unique
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### $\mat{A}$ singular

- row reduction has a missing pivot
- the homogeneous system is always consistent
- a nonpivot column gives a free variable

Choose the free variable(s) to obtain $\vct{z}\ne\vct{0}$ with

$$
\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
A singular action loses information: $\mat{A}(\vct{x}+t\vct{z})=\mat{A}\vct{x}$ for every $t$
:::

## The right-hand side decides

For singular square $\mat{A}$, the outcome of $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ depends on $\vct{b}$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Inconsistent

If elimination produces a contradiction,

$$
[\,0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c\,],
\qquad c\ne0,
$$

then there is [no solution]{.alert}
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Consistent

If $\vct{x}_0$ is one solution and $\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}$ with $\vct{z}\ne\vct{0}$, then

\begin{align*}
\mat{A}(\vct{x}_0+t\vct{z})
&=\mat{A}\vct{x}_0+t\mat{A}\vct{z}\\
&=\vct{b}+t\vct{0}=\vct{b}
\end{align*}

for every $t$: there are [infinitely many solutions]{.alert}
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
For singular square $\mat{A}$, no right-hand side gives exactly one solution: $\vct{b}$ determines none or infinitely many
:::

## Choose the least computation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### One or a few right-hand sides

Use Gaussian elimination and back substitution on

$$
[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}_1\ \cdots\ \vct{b}_k\,]
$$

Do not compute the entire inverse
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Many systems, same $\mat{A}$

Reuse the elimination structure or a factorization

Compute $\mat{A}^{-1}$ when the inverse itself is the object of interest
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Unnecessary computation costs time and creates more opportunities for round-off error
:::

---

### Elimination leaves reusable factors

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$ and $q=\min(m-1,n)$, suppose no row exchanges are needed:

$$
\mat{U}=\mat{M}_q\cdots\mat{M}_1\mat{A}
$$

Undoing the stages in reverse order gives

$$
\mat{A}=\mat{L}\mat{U},
\qquad
\mat{L}=\mat{M}_1^{-1}\cdots\mat{M}_q^{-1},
$$

These are the full-form factors: $\mat{L}\in\reals^{m\times m}$ is unit lower triangular, while $\mat{U}\in\reals^{m\times n}$ has zeros below its diagonal (and is upper triangular when square)

::: {.key-point}
[Matrix Transformations]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#elimination-becomes-a-factorization) will first develop this no-exchange LU example, then add a permutation matrix when row exchanges are needed
:::

# Leontief Input–Output Models

An economy must meet external demand while supporting its own production

- [Production creates internal demand](#production-creates-internal-demand)
- [One forecast or a response map?](#one-forecast-or-a-response-map)
- [Check the model, not only the arithmetic](#check-the-model-not-only-the-arithmetic)

## Production creates internal demand

Let

\begin{align*}
x_i & = \alerttext{gross production}\text{ of sector }i, \\
d_i & = \alerttext{external demand}\text{ for sector }i, \\
c_{ij} & = \text{output from sector }i\text{ needed per unit produced by sector }j.
\end{align*}

For all sectors at once,

$$
\underbrace{\vct{x}}_{\text{total}}
=\underbrace{\mat{C}\vct{x}}_{\text{internal}}
+\underbrace{\vct{d}}_{\text{external}}
$$

Therefore

$$
(\mat{I}-\mat{C})\vct{x}=\vct{d}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The solution $\vct{x}$ is the gross production plan required to meet $\vct{d}$. This is a [static balance model]{.alert}, not an optimization problem or a dynamic steady-state model.
:::

## One forecast or a response map?

Let

$$
\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}.20&.10\\.30&.25\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\vct{d}=\begin{bmatrix}72\\30\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### One demand forecast

Solve $(\mat{I}-\mat{C})\vct{x}=\vct{d}$ directly:

$$
\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}100\\80\end{bmatrix}
$$

This is the gross production required for the specified $\vct{d}$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Many possible demands

The response map is

$$
(\mat{I}-\mat{C})^{-1}
\approx
\begin{bmatrix}1.316&.175\\.526&1.404\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::
:::

## Check the model, not only the arithmetic

For $\vct{x}=(100,80)^{\mathsf T}$,

$$
\mat{C}\vct{x}+\vct{d}
=\begin{bmatrix}28\\50\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}72\\30\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}100\\80\end{bmatrix}
=\vct{x}
$$

- the inverse columns describe production responses to added demand
- nonnegative gross production is required for a meaningful plan
- if $\mat{I}-\mat{C}$ is singular, there is no unique response map

::: {.key-point}
Interpret the model before trusting the answer
:::

# Gaussian Covariance and Precision

A preview for later courses in statistics, AI, and data science—no statistics background is required

- [Covariance describes joint variation](#covariance-describes-joint-variation)
- [Precision describes conditional structure](#precision-describes-conditional-structure)
- [Compute a precision matrix](#compute-a-precision-matrix)

## Covariance describes joint variation

At selected inputs $t_1,\ldots,t_n$, a Gaussian-process model collects its values into a Gaussian vector:

$$
\vf=
\begin{bmatrix}
f(t_1)&\cdots&f(t_n)
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
\sim\Norm(\vmu,\mSigma),
\qquad
\mSigma_{ij}=K(t_i,t_j)
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Diagonal entries

$$
\mSigma_{ii}=\var(f(t_i))
$$

describe uncertainty at individual inputs
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Off-diagonal entries

$$
\mSigma_{ij}=\cov(f(t_i),f(t_j))
$$

describe how values at two inputs vary together
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
For now, remember the role: the square matrix $\mSigma$ records uncertainty and what varies together
:::

## Precision describes conditional structure

When $\mSigma$ is invertible, its [precision matrix]{.alert} is

$$
\mQ=\mSigma^{-1}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Statistical meaning

- $\vr^{\mathsf T}\mQ\vr$ weights a departure $\vr=\vf-\vmu$ relative to the expected joint variation
- for a Gaussian vector, $\mQ_{ij}=0$ means components $i$ and $j$ are conditionally independent given the others
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Computational meaning

If a calculation needs

$$
\valpha=\mQ\vr,
$$

solve

$$
\mSigma\valpha=\vr
$$

rather than forming $\mQ$
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
This is a preview, not a derivation to memorize. Covariance describes what varies together; precision describes conditional relationships and covariance-aware weighting.
:::

## Compute a precision matrix

$\exstar$ A Gaussian vector has covariance matrix

$$
\mSigma=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1&0\\
1&2&1\\
0&1&2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

1. Compute the precision matrix $\mQ=\mSigma^{-1}$ by Gauss--Jordan reduction of $[\,\mSigma\mid\mat{I}\,]$
2. Verify that $\mSigma\mQ=\mat{I}$
3. Compare $\mSigma_{13}$ with $\mQ_{13}$. What does this reveal about zeros in covariance and precision matrices?

::: {.notes}
Instructor result:

$$
\mQ=
\begin{bmatrix}
3&-2&1\\
-2&2&-1\\
1&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here $\mSigma_{13}=0$ but $\mQ_{13}=1$
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- An inverse [undoes a square matrix action]{.alert} on both sides: $\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{A}=\mat{I}=\mat{A}\mat{A}^{-1}$
- A square matrix is invertible exactly when row reduction produces an echelon form with [a pivot in every row and column]{.alert}; then $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ has exactly one solution for every $\vct{b}$
- [Gauss–Jordan reduction]{.alert} of $[\,\mat{A}\mid\mat{I}\,]$ computes $\mat{A}^{-1}$ when the inverse itself is needed
- Products undo in [reverse order]{.alert}; associativity permits regrouping, not reordering
- Use the [least computation]{.alert} the problem requires: solve directly for one or a few right-hand sides; form a reusable response map only when it is needed
- Applications give inverses meaning: a Leontief response map connects demand to production; Gaussian precision describes [conditional structure and covariance-aware weighting]{.alert}

$$
